Skip to the end of this for pro-tip. As far as I can tell (I work in the industry), Duckworth contracts smaller “cut-and-sew” operations to put together their shirt-jackets. That’s pretty cool actually! But that’s a huge part of their price point on these garments. I’m guessing they can’t get a larger US factory to take a contract for these shirts without higher costs…or at all…and…those operations would likely want to do one big run of jackets all at once and then not again for a year or more or ever again? So Duckworth would have to do what all other smaller quality/heritage/designer garment makers do…and have them sewn overseas, or start sewing themselves in-house, or invest in larger volume limited runs that…when they sell out, they sell out…and are gone for LONG periods of time, if they are ever made again at all. So contracting many small makers instead allows for a roving supply that can sustain more constant supply, but smaller number of orders of these shirts. So I’m guessing, I could be totally wrong, that this is the reason for their price point AND the reason for the bound edges inside the garment. The price point is intentionally high to keep the item slightly exclusive because production would not keep up with demand if they were $50-100 cheaper (you are correct that they could absolutely be sewn at the same quality and sold for a lower price with slight tweaks to their process). And the binding is to achieve consistency across numerous small shops–where getting consistency would be difficult for serged edges? I think they could totally switch to serged edge finish and embrace having subtle differences in the finished product. All they’d have to do is acknowledge how the meat is actually made (a very small amount) and take pride in it, and no one would care? BUT the BEST way…I’m looking at my family heirloom US Army wool shirt-jacket which has been worn for over 70 years and is in amazing shape…the cut edges are serged with a blanket stitch AND THEN are assembled with a flat felled seam! Even the sleeves! No exposed edge! And idk…at least 3 runs of tight stitching in every single seam. This would be hard to do today in the US. When this Army jacket was made there were many thousands of professional, industrial sewing machine operators with thousands of hours of experience running complex seams as standard practice…not anymore…kind of…definitely not for clothing. If Duckworth had somebody tweak their patterns and rebuild their assembly system for their shirt-jacket, I think they could totally run with the superior flat felled seam by using small sew shop contractors…but don’t break it if it isn’t fixed? Now for the extra mile: My red, vintage, union-sewn Filson coat is constructed the same way as the Army shirt-jacket, BUT the edge treatment is a blanket stitch of the exact same wool yarn as the fabric! So you can only see it with a bright light and a needle to move the fibers around. Now, if you can’t afford a Duckworth shirt-jacket, head over to eBay and search for “US army wool shirt-jacket,” or “army wool field shirt” (for the slightly lighter weight version with no reinforced shoulder/yoke seams and slightly smaller breast pockets) and buy one for $30-100 and machine wash it warm on a gentle cycle with a dab of liquid dish soap and tumble dry on low for 20 minutes, then lay flat to dry completely, then wear for the rest of your life.

Also, top marks on the Mammoth! A+ for the single color scheme. 100/100 for the label designs. I assumed you were a vintage label dork, but as a newcomer to your channel I don’t have any other data on that yet!
